name: read_scene
description: Read the current Creator scene. Returns scene dimensions, framerate, duration, all layers, current selection, render order, visual bounds, scene-center deltas, and clipping/off-canvas flags. Call this once at the start of most turns to understand what's on the canvas. Use each layer's `ordering` and `layout` blocks to avoid wrong-layer, wrong-stack, and off-canvas mistakes. A layer may also carry an `occlusion` block (`likely_hidden: true`, `occluded_by: [ids]`) when an opaque layer in front of it covers it — treat that layer as INVISIBLE on the canvas (e.g. a label buried behind a button fill); reorder it above the cover with `reorder_layer` before reporting done. No input required — always reads the active scene.

name: apply_keyframes
description: Add keyframes to ONE animatable property on ONE layer. This is the preferred tool for simple single-property animations (rotate, fade, slide, pulse, recolor). If you need to animate multiple properties on the same layer, plan separate tool calls in the order they should be applied; Creator serializes native tool execution through the dispatcher. **POLISH TURNS (snappier / smoother / tighter / less bouncy / fix timing / more premium / etc.) — call `read_keyframes` FIRST on every animated layer in scope BEFORE calling this tool.** The conversation history's view of existing keyframes is stale once the user edits in Creator directly; reading is the only safe source of truth. Then prefer the smallest possible mutation: easing-only change > retiming > amplitude tweak > full rebuild. See motion-design.md → 'Repair / polish protocol' for the full rule. Value type depends on the property: - `position`, `scale` → value is `{x, y}`. **`scale` is a percentage of the layer's AUTHORED size, matching AE / Creator semantics — NOT a percentage of 100.** A layer the user imported or hand-resized can sit at `50`, `200`, `1250`, etc. — and THAT value is the resting state. Animating a layer authored at 1250 → 110 collapses it to ~9% of its on-canvas size and looks like a bug. **Always read the current static value via `read_keyframes` or `read_scene` before writing scale keyframes**, then animate RELATIVE to that authored value (1250 pulses to 1350, not to 110). Same baseline rule applies to `position` and `rotation` — the layer's authored values are the resting state, not 0/0 or 0°. See motion-design.md → 'Baseline awareness'. **TEXT `position` is doubly dangerous: a text layer's transform anchor is the baseline / box origin, so its raw `position` value is NOT its `visual_center` and NOT the `position` arg you gave `create_text` (that arg is the visual center). Feeding `visual_center` in as a `position` keyframe throws the text off-canvas. For a settle-into-place entrance use `animate_entrance` (no coordinate needed); for any other text move, `read_keyframes` the raw `static_value` and animate RELATIVE to it. Never repair a keyframed text layer with `set_anchor_point` → `center_layer` — they stack two shifts and fling it off-canvas.** - `rotation`, `opacity` → value is a number (rotation in degrees; opacity 0–100) - `fill_color` → value is `{r, g, b}` with 0-255 per channel. **Requires a SOLID fill at `fills[0]`** — animation only works when the layer's first fill is SOLID. Gradient or empty layers will fail with `'Layer has no SOLID fill at fills[0]'`. To animate the color of a layer that currently has a gradient (or no fill), call `set_fill({type:'SOLID', color: <starting color>})` FIRST, then this tool. Verify the fill type via `read_scene` (look at the layer's fill metadata) or just call `set_fill` defensively before animating colors on a layer you didn't create with a solid fill. - `trim_start`, `trim_end` → number 0–100 (percent of path). Use for stroke draw-on reveals: animate `trim_end` from 0 → 100 to grow the path in. A trim path is auto-created on first use. If the current playhead stays at a frame where `trim_end` is 0 or opacity is 0, the layer is correctly present but invisible on canvas; after creating a reveal, call `set_current_frame` to leave Creator on a visible frame. - `trim_offset` → number 0–360 (degrees around the path). For rotating-around-path effects. - `stroke_width` → number (pixels). Requires the layer to already have a stroke — use `set_stroke` first. To set a static color (no animation), pass a single keyframe at frame 0 and consider `clear_first: true` to remove any existing color animation. Easing is optional on any keyframe; omit it for linear-ish default. Use `CUBIC_BEZIER` with explicit control points for polished motion; `LINEAR` for deliberate no-easing. Use `clear_first: true` to replace existing keyframes on that property; otherwise new keyframes are merged with existing ones (sorted by frame). For paint, shape geometry, masks, groups, scene settings, and timing edits, prefer the dedicated typed tools (`animate_paint`, `animate_property`, `create_shape_group`, `update_mask`, `retime_keyframes`) over rebuilding with many generic keyframe calls. **RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** returns `{ layer_id, property, added, total_after }`. `added` is how many keyframes THIS call submitted; **`total_after` is a real read-back of how many keyframes the property holds afterwards** — it is re-read from the layer, not echoed from your input. - **Write success:** the call did not throw and the requested value was read back. A non-throwing one-keyframe write with `total_after: 1` is a valid static write. - **Animation success:** motion requires at least two distinct stored keyframe frames. After a multi-keyframe submission, `total_after: 1` means the write collapsed and the layer will not animate; call `read_keyframes` if the returned count or frames are unexpected. - With `clear_first: true`, expect `total_after === added`. A LARGER number means keyframes you did not write survived on that property and the result is a blend of old and new — `read_keyframes` before reporting done. - Without `clear_first`, `total_after` is the merged count. If it is lower than (previous + `added`), some of your frames landed on frames that already had keyframes and replaced them rather than adding. - Throws (and writes NOTHING) on an unknown `layer_id`, on a property that is not animatable on that layer, and on an unknown easing PRESET `name`.

name: apply_motion_preset
description: Apply a Motion Preset from the user's Motion System to a single layer. A preset is a multi-property keyframe collection for supported layer transform properties (position + scale + rotation + opacity, any subset) with a duration. This bakes the preset's keyframes into the layer — there's NO link semantics, future preset edits don't propagate. Preset trimPath data is not currently baked by the native gateway; use `apply_keyframes` on `trim_start`/`trim_end` for stroke reveals. Use this when the user names a preset (e.g. 'apply our brand entrance to this card'). For single-property motion (just an easing, just a duration), use `list_motion_system_items` + the existing keyframe tools instead — presets are the multi-property shortcut. **Mode** defaults to `'replace'` — this is what the user almost always wants. 'replace' clears existing keyframes on the preset's target properties first, then bakes the preset in. Only pass `'add'` when the user explicitly says 'on top of', 'in addition to', 'while keeping', 'compose with', or similar layering language. In `'add'` mode existing keyframes are preserved and the preset's absolute values are inserted with their frames shifted to the current playhead; scale/rotation/opacity are not added relative to the layer's current authored values. 'apply our brand entrance' = `'replace'`; 'apply our brand entrance while keeping the existing wobble' = `'add'`. Returns `{ layer_id, preset_id, preset_label, mode, duration_ms, affected_properties, applied_properties, readback }`. Success means the target layer was read back with changed, meaningful animated keyframes: at least one applied property has 2 or more distinct keyframe frames. Throws on unknown preset_id, unknown layer_id, presets with no meaningful supported motion, or actor no-ops/incompatible targets where no meaningful keyframes were actually created. If only some preset properties apply, inspect `applied_properties` and `readback` before describing the result to the user.

name: apply_motion_path
description: Make a layer's position FOLLOW a path shape — Creator's 'apply path to motion' feature. Each vertex of the path becomes a position keyframe and the path's bezier in/out tangents become the keyframe's spatial tangents, so the layer curves smoothly along the path instead of jumping in straight-line segments between waypoints. **Reach for this when the user wants a custom curving motion** — 'have the ball arc over the obstacle', 'make the icon trace an S-curve', 'follow this road', 'orbit around the logo', 'fly across the scene'. The path is a regular path shape created via `create_shape`/`bend_shape` (or any existing path in the scene). The motion is whatever curve the path describes. The tool writes SpatialKeyframes (the same primitive Creator's motion-path editor produces), which is the only way to get smooth curved motion between waypoints. Hand-authoring position keyframes via `apply_keyframes` gives straight-line interpolation between frames — fine for ramps and pulses, wrong for anything 'curve along this shape'. **Framing — the path must be centered on the scene:** - Read scene size first (`read_scene`). Set the path layer's `position` to the scene CENTER (e.g. `{ x: 256, y: 256 }` for 512×512). Author vertex positions as signed displacements from that center, capped at roughly ±(scene_size/2 − 40) so the motion stays inside the viewport with a margin (so x ∈ [−216, +216] on a 512-wide scene). - World motion coords are `layer.position + vertex`. If the target ends up off-canvas, either the layer wasn't centered or a vertex is past the viewport bound. Tangents can extend past the bound — only vertex anchor points need to stay inside. **Use TWO vertices for an S-curve, not three.** A 2-anchor bezier with strong opposing tangents produces a smooth flowing S; adding a middle vertex constrains the curve and tends to read as a zig-zag. Only use 3+ vertices when the user explicitly asks for a 'sharp' or 'kinked' S, or when the path has multiple distinct turns. **Tangent rules — get this right or the curve renders as a polyline:** - Tangent magnitude ≈ 30–50% of the distance to the adjacent vertex. Smaller flattens; larger loops. - For a smooth pass-through at any intermediate vertex, that vertex's inTan and outTan must be ANTI-PARALLEL — `outTan = -inTan`. Any other combo produces a visible corner. - For a TWO-vertex S, the start's outTan-y and the end's inTan-y must have OPPOSITE SIGNS (e.g. start outTan = (120, -150), end inTan = (-120, 150)). That sign flip is what creates the S inflection. Same-sign tangents produce an arc. - See `motion-patterns.md` → 'S-curve recipe' for a worked 2-vertex example. Prerequisites: - `path_layer_id` points to a SHAPE_LAYER containing exactly one path shape with at least 2 vertices, OR to a path shape directly. - `target_layer_id` points to any transformable layer (shape, text, image, precomp). - Both layers must be in the active scene. Defaults: - `constant_speed: true` distributes the keyframes by arc length, so the motion is uniform along the curve (vs. evenly spaced in time, which makes long path segments visibly speed up). Leave it on unless the user asks for 'ease into corners'. - **`auto_orient`: pass `true` whenever the verb implies directional motion** — 'fly', 'follow', 'swoop', 'travel', 'tour', 'drive', 'race', 'trace'. The target rotates to face the direction of travel for the entire path. Only leave `auto_orient: false` when the user explicitly wants the layer to keep its original orientation (e.g. 'slide along the path without rotating'). - `remove_source: true` deletes the source path layer after applying (the agent typically drew it as scaffolding). Pass `false` to keep the path visible in the scene.

name: set_anchor_point
description: Move a layer's ANCHOR POINT — the pivot for rotation and scale. Mirrors Creator's property-panel 9-grid anchor selector. Compensates the layer's position so the visible rendering DOES NOT JUMP when the anchor moves; if position is animated, every position keyframe shifts together so the motion shape is preserved. **Reach for this BEFORE animating rotation or scale** whenever the verb implies a specific pivot: - 'door opens / swings from the left hinge' → `direction: 'left'`, then animate rotation - 'drawer slides down from the top' / 'curtain drops' → `direction: 'top'`, then animate scale.y - 'pendulum / clock hand / chandelier swing' → `direction: 'top'`, then rotation - 'standing thing falls over' (tips on its base) → `direction: 'bottom'`, then rotation - 'pop in from the corner' / 'punch in from the bottom-right' → `direction: 'bottom-right'`, then scale + opacity - 'flag flapping from the pole on the left' → `direction: 'left'`, then rotation/skew **Critical: set the anchor BEFORE adding the rotation/scale keyframes.** Setting it AFTER moves where those existing keyframes pivot — the layer will appear to lurch because each frame's render uses the new pivot but the keyframed values were authored against the old one. Stage the anchor, then animate. Pass EXACTLY ONE of: - `direction`: one of 9 presets (top-left, top, top-right, left, center, right, bottom-left, bottom, bottom-right). The gateway maps to the corresponding corner / edge / midpoint of the layer's local bounding box. - `position`: raw `{x, y}` in layer-local pixels for custom placement (e.g. matching a specific anchor on a complex shape). If the layer has no clear bounding box (rare — text and shape layers always have one), the gateway falls back to a 100×100 box centered on local origin, so `direction` still gives sensible results.

name: create_shape
description: **BEFORE CALLING: check the creation order.** New layers are inserted at the TOP of the render stack. If this turn creates multiple layers, emit the calls in BOTTOM→TOP order — the background FIRST, the foreground LAST. A card background MUST be created BEFORE its content; a sky rectangle MUST be created BEFORE the logo on it. (Reorder APIs exist if needed via `reorder_layer`, but planning the order is cheaper.) Create a new shape layer with a vector primitive. Supports rectangle, ellipse, polygon (regular N-gon), star, and arbitrary bezier path. By default it gets a solid fill (`fill_color`, or gray if omitted). For a RING / outline / donut, pass `fill_color: "none"` + `stroke: { color, width }` — that's a stroke-only shape in ONE call. You can also combine a fill AND a stroke. Returns `layer_id` so you can immediately animate it with `apply_keyframes`. If the user asks for several shapes at once, emit one tool call per shape in the intended render order; Creator serializes native tool execution. **Position is the VISUAL CENTER for every primitive (rectangle, ellipse, polygon, star).** `path` is positioned at the layer origin and extends as its `path.points` define. A rectangle with `size: {512, 512}` at `position: {x:0, y:0}` in a 512×512 scene shows ONLY the bottom-right quadrant — its center is pinned to the scene's top-left corner. To cover that scene the position must be `{x:256, y:256}` (the rectangle's center → the scene's center). **BEFORE you reach for `fill_scene: true` — STOP. Do you actually need an exported background layer?** Motion-design convention: animations float on transparency so they composite anywhere. The exported Lottie keeps a transparent background — adding a full-scene rectangle BAKES IN a color the user almost never wants in the final file. The three valid reasons to add a background SHAPE LAYER: (1) gradient/multi-stop background that IS the design, (2) contrast genuinely unsolvable any other way, (3) the user EXPLICITLY says "add a background layer". For ALL other cases — including "premium dashboard", "dark mode preview", "card on a tinted backdrop" — use **`set_scene_background({ color })`** instead. That changes Creator's preview tint WITHOUT polluting the export. See motion-aesthetics → "NO BACKGROUND LAYER BY DEFAULT". `fill_scene: true` is for the narrow case where one of the three valid reasons above actually applies. The native tool reads the active scene's dimensions and sets `size` + `position` correctly. Only supported for `rectangle`. Parameter shape is a discriminated field — provide the params for the chosen shape: - `shape: "rectangle"` → `size: { width, height }` OR `fill_scene: true`. Optional `roundness` (px) — set this for ANY card/panel/modal/button; default-sharp corners read as wireframe. - `shape: "ellipse"` → `size: { width, height }`. - `shape: "polygon"` → `points` (number of sides, ≥3), `outer_radius` OR `size`, optional `outer_roundness` (0-100) - `shape: "star"` → `points` (≥3), `outer_radius` + `inner_radius` OR `size` (inner defaults to half outer), optional `outer_roundness` / `inner_roundness` (0-100 each) - `shape: "path"` → `path: { points: [{vertex:{x,y}, inTan:{x,y}, outTan:{x,y}}, ...], closed: boolean }` Use one tool call per shape. 'Three circles stacked vertically' = 3 serialized create_shape calls.

name: bend_shape
description: Bend one edge of an existing rectangle/square-like SHAPE_LAYER by replacing its first shape with a 5-point bezier path, OR animate an already-bent path by keyframing its pathData. Use this for prompts like 'bend the top of this square', 'curve the bottom edge', 'bow the card inward', or 'animate the bend'. Static bend: pass `amount` (typical 8-24px). Animated bend: pass `animate: true`; the tool reuses an existing bent PATH shape when present, infers its bounds, and writes pathData keyframes directly. Do NOT fake bend animation with scale keyframes. `tangent_width` controls how broad/smooth the curve is; default 60.

name: create_text
description: **BEFORE CALLING: check the creation order.** New text layers are inserted at the TOP of the render stack. If this turn also creates a card / background / banner, create the background FIRST and THIS text layer LAST — otherwise the text will land beneath the background. (Reorder APIs exist if needed via `reorder_layer`, but planning the order is cheaper.) Create a new native TEXT_LAYER with the given content and optional native TextDocument style. Returns `layer_id` so you can immediately animate it with `apply_keyframes` (opacity for fade-in, position for slide, scale for pop). For letter-by-letter or word-by-word staggered animations, emit one text-layer call per unit in the order they should be created; Creator serializes native tool execution. **Centering is by VISUAL BOUNDS, not layer origin.** Use `center_in_scene: true` for scene center. Use `position: {x,y}` when you want the bounds center at a specific target point (e.g. top-center hero text). Do not manually compensate for text origin/anchor. **For long body copy that needs to wrap, pass `wrap_width` instead of constructing a text box yourself.** The gateway translates `wrap_width` into a centered wrap box internally — your `position` / `center_in_scene` still controls visual placement. `wrap_width` without an explicit `align` uses center alignment; pass `align: "left"` for a conventional paragraph column. Omit `wrap_width` for headlines, subtitles, footers, single-line text. Native text styling supports font size, font family/variant or font name, fill color, stroke color/width, alignment, line height, tracking, caps, and `wrap_width`. For "slight tracking", use a small value such as 2-8; values around 20-40 are very wide and can make title text exceed the scene. **RESPONSE — verify these BEFORE saying "Done":** - `visual_center` is where the rendered text actually centers. Compare against your intent (`position` or scene center). - `visual_bounds` is the rendered rectangle in world coords. - `scene_fit.clipped` / `scene_fit.off_canvas` / `scene_fit.overflow.{left,right,top,bottom}`: if any overflow > 0, the new text is clipped at the canvas edge. Self-correct (reduce `font_size`, add `wrap_width`, shorten the text) or surface the limitation in one short line. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

name: create_text_group
description: **USE THIS for any prompt that asks for 2+ text layers as a coherent composition** — hero slides, title+subtitle+footer, label+value pairs, multi-line callouts. One tool call lays out the whole group with sensible typography defaults and centers it on the scene as a unit. Why this exists: composing the same layout out of `create_text` + `align_layer` typically takes 6-15 tool calls (create each, align each, shrink if clipped, re-center). This tool runs the equivalent sequence server-side with one response, picking Cal Sans (the project default), role-derived sizes (H2 = ½ × H1), and the correct typography color hierarchy. **Roles** drive font_size + font_variant + fill_color + line-height + tracking when you don't override them (Slate ramp, never pure black; display headings get NEGATIVE tracking so they read tight, not loose): - `h1` → big bold slate-900 (the main title), tight leading, negative tracking - `h2` → half of H1, slate-600 (subtitle), slight negative tracking - `h3` → ~40% of H1, slate-600 - `body` → ~36% of H1, slate-600, neutral tracking - `caption` / `footer` → ~28% of H1, slate-500 (muted but readable) If you omit `role`, the position picks it: first item = h1, second = h2, rest = body. So `items: [{ text: 'Welcome' }, { text: 'Get started' }, { text: 'lottiefiles.com' }]` Just Works. **Sizing**: `font_size` defaults scale with the scene size — on a 512×512 canvas H1 ≈ 44px; on a 1080×1080 canvas H1 ≈ 80px. Override `font_size` per item only when the design specifically calls for it. **Layout**: `vstack-centered` (the only mode for now) stacks items vertically with `gap` pixels between, centered horizontally on the scene, with the group's vertical center landing on `scene_anchor`. `scene_anchor: 'center'` (default) centers the whole stack. `'top-center'` biases it to the upper third; `'bottom-center'` to the lower third. Pass `{x, y}` for an arbitrary anchor. **RESPONSE**: returns `items: [{ layer_id, text, visual_center, visual_bounds, ... }, ...]`, `group_visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit` for the whole group. Check `scene_fit.clipped` and adjust the largest `font_size` once if the group overflowed — don't loop guessing sizes.

name: create_button
description: Build a button / pill / chip in ONE call. Composes a rounded fill panel + a CENTERED label + optical padding (vertical < horizontal) + a WCAG-AA contrast-correct label color + correct z-order (label in front) + an auto elevation, grouped into one animatable precomp. **Use this instead of hand-rolling `create_shape` + `create_text` + `reorder_layer`** for any button/pill/chip/CTA/tag. It can't get the z-order, padding, radius, or label contrast wrong, and you never have to reference a layer id you're still creating. `variant`: `button` (md/8 radius), `pill` (stadium — auto-clamps to half the shorter side), `chip` (smaller, md/8). `fill_color` defaults to Slate-700 `{r:51,g:65,b:85}`; pass a REAL RGB object for an explicit CTA color, or `fill_color:'none'` + a `stroke` for an outlined button. Do not pass stringified JSON. `fill` is only an optional named Flat-UI accent string (e.g. 'peter-river') and is ignored when `fill_color` is provided. The **label color is auto-picked** (slate-50 vs slate-900, whichever clears AA on the fill) — only pass `label_color` to override, and it's kept only if it still passes AA. `elevation`: a tier (`resting`/`raised`/`floating`), or `false`/`'none'` to suppress the auto-resting lift. Returns `{ button_layer_id (the group), panel_layer_id, label_layer_id, label_color, contrast_ratio, passes_aa, visual_center, visual_bounds }` — animate the whole button via `button_layer_id` (e.g. `animate_entrance`).

name: create_reference_board
description: Build a whole multi-section REFERENCE BOARD in ONE call — a title plus a stack of labelled sections. **This is the right tool for "illustrate my motion system", a style guide, a color-palette board, a token/spec sheet, an icon or feature list, or any reference overview.** Do NOT hand-place a board out of many `create_text` + `create_shape` calls — that scatters off-center, drops sections off-grid, and floats the title in the middle (the #1 failure mode). This composes everything into ONE `layout` column (origin scene-center), so the board is centered, evenly gapped, edge-aligned, safe-zone-fit, and on-canvas BY CONSTRUCTION. Each `section` has an optional `heading` and ONE content kind: `swatches` (color chips — a compact bare grid, or a {swatch,label} legend when ≤8 chips carry `label`s), `rows` ({label,value} spec rows), or `lines` (text specimens like font samples or easing values). Returns the composed `layout` result (`items`, `cascade_order` for `stagger_layers`, `content_bounds`, `created_layer_ids`).

name: set_text
description: Update the text content of an existing TEXT_LAYER using native TextDocument APIs. By default the tool preserves the current visual bounds center after the text changes, so the layer does not jump when the new string is wider or narrower. **RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** returns `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit`. A string swap can push the new bounds past the canvas edge — check `scene_fit.clipped` / `scene_fit.overflow.{left,right,top,bottom}` after EVERY set_text. If anything overflows, self-correct (downscale `font_size` via `set_text_style`, add `wrap_width` via `set_text_style` for paragraph copy, or shorten the text) or surface the limitation in one short line. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

name: set_text_style
description: Update native TextDocument styling on an existing TEXT_LAYER. Supports font size, font family/variant or font name, fill color, stroke color/width, alignment, line height, tracking, caps, and `wrap_width` (for paragraph copy that needs to wrap inside a fixed-width column). Setting `wrap_width` without an explicit `align` uses center alignment; pass `align: "left"` to keep a conventional paragraph column. Pass `fill_color: null` to clear the fill override, `stroke_color: null` to clear the stroke color override, and `stroke_width: null` to clear the stroke width override. By default it preserves the current visual bounds center after style changes. For "slight tracking", use 2-8, not 20-40. **RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** returns `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit`. Bumping `font_size` can push the rendered text past the canvas edge — check `scene_fit.clipped` / `scene_fit.overflow.{left,right,top,bottom}` after EVERY set_text_style call. If anything overflows, self-correct (smaller multiplier, add `wrap_width` to wrap, or bump the scene via `set_scene_settings`) or surface the limitation in one short line. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

name: measure_text_units
description: Return per-line, per-word, and per-character bounds for an existing text layer. Uses the same canvas.measureText pipeline that powers `read_scene`'s `measured_bounds`, but exposes the cumulative pen position per glyph so per-character recipes can place each new layer at the source's exact kerning — no `bounds.width / char_count` approximation. When to call (REQUIRED before splitting): - Any per-character recipe (typewriter, per-character-rise, bottom-up-letters, top-down-letters, kinetic-center-build, short-slide-*). - Any per-word recipe where each word needs its own layer (per-word-crossfade, spring-scale-in) so the rebuilt phrase reads as one centered unit. - Layout-aware effects that need exact word widths (short-slide-down, short-slide-right, kinetic-center-build). When NOT to call: - Whole-layer recipes (micro-scale-fade, fade-through, scale-down-fade, mask-reveal-up) — those animate one layer; `read_scene`'s `visual_bounds` is enough. - Layers that aren't text — call returns an error. Returns (positions match `read_scene`'s coordinate system): - `local_bounds` / `world_bounds` for the whole layer (matches `text_style.measured_bounds` and `layout.visual_bounds` from `read_scene`). - `font`: `{ name, size, tracking, line_height, alignment }` — pass these to `create_text` per character/word/line to preserve the source typeface. - `lines[]`: one entry per `\n`-separated line. Each line carries `text`, `local_bounds`, `world_bounds`, and optionally `words[]` / `characters[]` depending on `granularity`. - `characters[i].local_bounds.x + width/2` is the visual CENTER of glyph i; use that as the `position.x` for the per-character layer. - `characters[i].advance_x_local` is the pen position AFTER glyph i (left edge of glyph i+1 with tracking applied). Sum across glyphs and you reproduce the line width. Granularity: - `line` — only line bounds. Cheapest. Use for per-line recipes. - `word` — adds word bounds inside each line. Use for per-word recipes. - `character` — adds character bounds inside each line. Use for per-character recipes. - `all` (default) — words + characters. Cheap; the heavy lifting is already done. Limits: - Measurement uses the active document fonts. If the layer's font hasn't loaded yet, widths fall back to a coarse `0.48 * fontSize` estimate (returned as one-line/zero-words/zero-characters in non-DOM contexts). Verify with `inspect_scene` if you suspect a font-load race. - The returned positions are in the same coordinate space as `read_scene` — `local_bounds` is relative to the layer's anchor (alignment already applied), `world_bounds` is in scene coordinates.

name: split_text
description: Split a text layer into one new text layer per character, word, or line at exact `measure_text_units` positions. Copies the source font/style to every new layer and (by default) deletes the source so the new layers don't render on top of the original. Replaces the manual `measure_text_units` → `delete_layer` → loop-of-create_text dance. When to call: - Any per-character recipe (typewriter, per-character-rise, bottom-up-letters, top-down-letters) — pass `granularity: 'character'`. - Any per-word recipe (per-word-crossfade, spring-scale-in) — pass `granularity: 'word'`. - Any per-line recipe (line-by-line-slide, mask-reveal-up) — pass `granularity: 'line'`. When NOT to call: - Whole-layer animations — there's only one layer; nothing to split. - You need different fonts per unit — split with `copy_style: false` then `set_text_style` per layer. - You want to animate the original AND a split copy — pass `delete_source: false`. Returns `{ source_layer_id, source_deleted, granularity, layers: [{ layer_id, text, position: {x,y}, bounds }] }`. The `layers` array is in reading order (line 0 first, then line 1, …) so you can iterate with a running stagger index. Each `position` is the visual center of the unit in scene coordinates — already aligned with what `create_text` does when called with that position, so no `center_layer` follow-up is needed. Limits: - Up to ~80 units per call. Beyond that the per-create dispatch overhead dominates; consider `granularity: 'word'` instead of 'character' on long copy. - Splits are sequential, not transactional today — N undo steps, not one. Plan accordingly when chaining with other edits. - Spaces ARE returned as their own layers when `granularity: 'character'` (their bounds may be zero-width). Skip them client-side if your recipe doesn't animate them, but keep the layer count exact if your stagger formula uses `i` as the index.

name: stagger_layers
description: Apply a staggered entrance to MANY existing layers in ONE call — each layer enters slightly after the previous, reading as one cascading sequence. This replaces the per-layer `set_anchor_point` + 2×`apply_keyframes` loop (≈3N calls) that the agent used to hand-roll for letter cascades, card grids, list reveals, etc. The stagger reads EACH layer's own resting position, so it's safe on already-distinct layers (split-text letters at their kerned spots, grid cards at their slots) — unlike `copy_animation`, which would copy one layer's absolute position onto all the others and collapse them into a single spot. Layer order in `layer_ids` IS the cascade order. Each layer gets a frame-0 hold so it stays invisible/offset until its turn (no 'everything visible at frame 0' bug). Returns `{ staggered, last_entrance_end_frame, ... }` — use `last_entrance_end_frame` to place the NEXT beat (subtitle, button) so the whole scene reads as one composed sequence. For 'letters slide up with a 10-frame stagger', either call `split_text` with its `animate` option (one call total), or split then call this with `{ preset: 'slide', direction: 'up', per_item_delay_frames: 10 }`.

name: animate_entrance
description: Animate ONE layer's entrance (a settle-into-place reveal) WITHOUT supplying any position coordinate. The tool reads the layer's OWN resting transform and animates relative to it, so the layer settles back EXACTLY where it rests. **This is the SAFE path for a TEXT reveal.** A text layer's `position` keyframes live in RAW transform (baseline / box-origin) space — which is DIFFERENT from `visual_center` and from the `position` arg you passed to `create_text` (that arg is the visual center). Reusing the visual center as a `position` keyframe value silently throws the text off-canvas (the cause of a 30-call, 3-rebuild logo-reveal failure). `animate_entrance` takes no coordinate, so that mistake is impossible. Use it right after creating a layer to give it a premium entrance. `style`: `rise` (slide up into place, position only), `rise-fade` (slide + fade, the default), `fade` (opacity only), `scale` (grow from a centered anchor + fade). It only SETTLES the layer to its current resting spot — it is not a relocate, and it must NOT be re-run on a layer that already has position keyframes. Do NOT chain `set_anchor_point` or `center_layer` before/after it. For MANY layers cascading, use `stagger_layers`. For a non-entrance move along a path, read the raw `static_value` via `read_keyframes` and use `apply_keyframes` relative to it. Returns `{ layer_id, style, entrance_start_frame, entrance_end_frame, duration_frames }` — use `entrance_end_frame` to time the next beat.

name: list_fonts
description: List font families available in the active project — Creator's curated presets, Google Fonts, OS-installed local fonts (when permission has been granted), and project-uploaded font assets. Use this when the user names a specific font you're not sure is loaded ('animate "Acme" in Bebas Neue letter-by-letter'), or when you need to recommend a fallback that's actually present. When to call: - User names a font you're not certain exists in this project (brand fonts, niche typefaces). - You're about to call `create_text` / `set_text_style` with a specific `font_name` and want to verify the family + style are loaded. - You're deciding between multiple style options for the same family. When NOT to call: - The user didn't specify a font — `create_text` uses the project default. Calling this would just burn a turn. - You already called it earlier in the conversation. Returns `{ families: [{ family, styles, default_style, source }] }`. `source` is one of `'PRESET' | 'GOOGLE_FONT' | 'LOCAL' | 'ASSET'`. If the requested family isn't in the list, fall back to a similar style + tell the user (e.g. 'Bebas Neue isn't loaded; I used Anton, the closest condensed sans available'). Pass `source` to filter to one category. Note: the catalog is a snapshot of what's currently loaded. Local OS fonts only appear after the user grants the browser's `local-fonts` permission, which Creator does not prompt for automatically.

name: center_layer
description: Reposition an EXISTING layer so its visual center lands on a SPECIFIC target point (e.g. a callout at `(180, 380)`, or anywhere off-center). For text, this uses rendered bounds when Creator has them and measured text bounds otherwise, so it avoids the top-left/origin centering bug. **For aligning to scene center (the common case), use `align_layer({ direction: 'horizontal-center' })` + `align_layer({ direction: 'vertical-center' })` instead — that's Creator's own alignment path and the more reliable default.** Use `center_layer` only when the target is not the scene center. For a brand-new centered text layer, prefer `create_text` with `center_in_scene: true`. **RESPONSE — verify before saying "Done":** - `target_reached` is the authoritative placement result: `true` only when both an independent rendered-bounds check and the returned `visual_center` match the target within ~1px; `false` when a rendered verification result exists but its center misses, or the returned `visual_center` is unavailable or misses; and `undefined` when no target or rendered verification result is available, including unavailable bounds, verification errors, or the 1,500ms timeout. **If it is not `true`**: retry with `align_layer` (which uses Creator's authoritative alignment math), OR surface the limitation to the user in one short line. - `visual_center` may be the projected post-mutation center while rendering settles. Use it to understand the returned layout, not as proof that the move landed. - For text layers the response intentionally omits `position` — the layer's transform anchor sits at the baseline/box origin, not the visual center. - `scene_fit` also returned so you can confirm the layer didn't end up clipped. See motion-design.md → "Post-mutation layout integrity".

name: set_fill
description: Set (or replace) the fill on a SHAPE_LAYER. Supports SOLID colors AND linear/radial gradients. **Picking a default color (no brand defined, no mood specified):** check `list_slots` and `list_motion_system_items` first. If both empty and the user didn't name a color, stay MONOCHROME — Slate-700 `{r:51,g:65,b:85}` for accents / buttons, Slate-50 `{r:248,g:250,b:252}` for surfaces. Indigo / purple / pink / teal as defaults read as AI slop. When the user DOES name a color or mood, pick from the Flat UI defo palette (see `motion-aesthetics` skill) instead of inventing Tailwind values. ONE chromatic accent + neutrals; no rainbow palettes. **Defaults to replacing `fills[0]`.** Pass `replace_first: false` to append as a second fill instead. Color stops: each stop has `offset` (0–1, position along the gradient line), `color` ({r,g,b} 0–255), and optional `opacity` (0–1, default 1). Keep stop count modest (2–5 stops typical). For premium 'glow' effects fade the color to pure black and set blend mode with `set_blend_mode`. **Gradient geometry — `start` / `end` are PIXEL coordinates in layer-local space (NOT normalized 0–1 ratios).** The shape primitive sits at the layer's local origin (0, 0); a rectangle/ellipse with size {W, H} extends from (-W/2, -H/2) to (+W/2, +H/2). The gradient line runs from `start` to `end`; offset 0 is at `start`, offset 1 is at `end`. Common patterns for a centered shape with size {W, H}: | Direction | start | end | | ---------------- | -------------- | -------------- | | Top → bottom | {x:0, y:-H/2} | {x:0, y:H/2} | | Bottom → top | {x:0, y:H/2} | {x:0, y:-H/2} | | Left → right | {x:-W/2, y:0} | {x:W/2, y:0} | | Diagonal TL→BR | {x:-W/2, y:-H/2}| {x:W/2, y:H/2}| | Radial center-out| {x:0, y:0} | {x:W/2, y:0} | **Omit `start`/`end` entirely if you don't have a strong opinion** — the native tool computes sensible pixel defaults from the layer's bounds (linear: top→bottom; radial: center→edge). Do NOT pass {0, 0}–{0, 1} or {0.5, 0}–{0.5, 1} thinking those are 'normalized' coordinates: those would render the gradient inside a 1-pixel strip and you'll see only the first stop's color across the entire shape. - Radial-only: `highlightAngle` (degrees) and `highlightLength` (-100 to 100) shift the focal point off-center. To animate paint, use `animate_paint` for gradient stops/handles or `apply_keyframes` with `fill_color` for SOLID color cycles. `set_fill` is for changing the static fill kind.

name: set_stroke
description: Set (or replace) the stroke on a SHAPE_LAYER. Mirror of `set_fill` but for outlines/lines, plus a `width` (pixels). Supports SOLID and gradient strokes (same stop structure as set_fill). Defaults to replacing `strokes[0]`. Pass `replace_first: false` to append. After the stroke exists, you can animate its width over time with `apply_keyframes` property 'stroke_width'.

name: animate_paint
description: Keyframe fill or stroke paint directly. Use this for true animated gradients: create/ensure a gradient fill or stroke, then animate `gradient_stops`, `gradient_start`, `gradient_end`, or radial highlight properties. Use `solid_color` for a SOLID paint color cycle. This is the preferred tool for prompts like 'add animated gradients', 'make the gradient sweep', or 'animate the stroke colors'.

name: animate_property
description: Keyframe extended properties not covered by apply_keyframes, including paint opacity/color, gradient handles, shape geometry, mask path/opacity, text animator colors, and scene-layer time mapping. Use this when the property is explicitly named and a typed high-level tool is not a better fit. **Which sub-object gets animated** — the `property` picks a list on the layer, and `target_id`/`target_index` pick one entry in that list. **Both are optional and default to the FIRST entry**, which is what you want on the common single-mask / single-fill / single-shape layer: - `mask_path`, `mask_opacity` → the layer's masks (id from `create_mask`). - `shape_path`, `shape_size`, `rectangle_roundness`, `outer_radius`, `inner_radius`, `outer_roundness`, `inner_roundness`, `polygon_points`, `star_points` → the layer's shapes (id from `add_shape_to_layer`). - `stroke_color`, `stroke_opacity` → the layer's strokes; `fill_opacity`, `gradient_stops`, `gradient_start`, `gradient_end`, `highlight_angle`, `highlight_length` → the layer's fills, falling back to strokes when there is no matching fill. - `text_fill_color`, `text_stroke_color`, `text_stroke_width` → the layer's text animators (falls back to the layer itself when it has none). - `time_mapping` → the layer itself; both targeting fields are ignored. **RESPONSE:** returns `{ layer_id, property, target_index, target_id, added, total_after }`. `total_after` is a read-back of the keyframe count on the resolved property — treat `total_after >= 2` as the success predicate for an animation. Throws when the property is not available on the resolved target (e.g. `mask_path` on a layer with no masks).

name: set_blend_mode
description: Set a layer's blend mode. One of: normal, multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, color-dodge, color-burn, hard-light, soft-light, difference, exclusion, hue, saturation, color, luminosity. Common uses: - `screen` → glow / shine / highlight layers (fades to black = invisible) - `multiply` → shadows / darkening overlays - `overlay` / `soft-light` → color tinting - `difference` → inverting effects

name: add_drop_shadow
description: Attach a native Drop Shadow effect to a layer. Renders in Creator's preview and in dotlottie-web (the default Lottie player). lottie-web silently drops it. Use for: card/panel shadows, button lift, soft glow (distance=0 + large blur), text shadow. **Replaces the legacy 'duplicate dark rectangle behind the card' workaround** — call this instead. **Prefer `elevation` for UI surfaces.** Pass `elevation:'resting'|'raised'|'floating'` to attach a tuned TWO-shadow stack (a tight contact shadow + a soft ambient one, slate-tinted) in one call — this reads far more premium than a single hand-tuned shadow. `resting` = a card at rest, `raised` = hover/lifted, `floating` = modal/popover. When `elevation` is set the manual color/opacity/angle/distance/blur are ignored. Manual single-shadow param tips (when NOT using `elevation`): - `color` defaults to black {r:0,g:0,b:0}. Tint toward dark slate {r:15,g:23,b:42} for premium UI shadows. - `opacity` is 0-255 (Lottie convention). 191 ≈ 75% (default). 64 ≈ 25% for subtle, 230 ≈ 90% for dramatic. - `angle` in degrees, 135 = bottom-right (default). 90 = straight down, 270 = straight up. - `distance` in px. 0 = no offset (creates a soft glow). 4-8 = resting card. 12-24 = floating/modal lift. - `blur` in px. 0-2 = hard shadow. 8-15 = soft. 20-40 = very soft. Default 20.

name: add_blur
description: Attach a native Gaussian Blur effect to a layer. Renders in Creator's preview and in dotlottie-web. lottie-web silently drops it. Use for: blurred backgrounds, focus/defocus effects, soft glow with drop_shadow distance=0, glassy/frosted surfaces. Param tips: - `sigma` (px): blur strength. 5-10 = subtle, 15-25 = noticeable, 30-60 = dreamy/dramatic. Default 20. - `direction`: 0 = both axes (default), 1 = horizontal only, 2 = vertical only. - `wrap`: 0 = clamp edges (default, normal). 1 = repeat. Almost always leave at 0.

name: add_color_overlay
description: Attach a native Fill effect that overlays a solid color on the layer (multiply-style recolor). Renders in dotlottie-web; lottie-web drops it. Use for: recoloring imported SVG/image content without editing the source paths, hover-state overlays, themed tints. For shape layers you usually want `set_fill` instead — this is for cases where the layer's intrinsic fill should stay and a color washes over it. Param tips: - `color` required, RGB 0-255. - `opacity` 0-1 (Lottie Fill convention, not 0-255). Default 1 (full overlay).

name: add_tint
description: Attach a native Tint effect (two-color recolor: dark pixels → black color, light pixels → white color, with adjustable intensity). Renders in dotlottie-web; lottie-web drops it. Use for: duotone treatments, retro/poster looks, single-color overlays that preserve luminance variation. NOT for replacing a single fill color — use `set_fill` for that. Param tips: - `black` color maps to the darkest pixels (default {0,0,0}). - `white` color maps to the brightest pixels (default {255,255,255}). - `intensity` 0-100: 0 = no effect, 100 = full duotone replacement (default 100).

name: add_tritone
description: Attach a native Tritone effect (three-color recolor: highlight + midtone + shadow). Renders in dotlottie-web; lottie-web drops it. Use for: cinematic color grading, three-tone aesthetic treatments (sepia, vintage, dusk), branded recolors with more depth than `add_tint`. Param tips: - `highlight` color maps to brightest pixels (default white). - `midtone` color maps to middle luminance (default gray). - `shadow` color maps to darkest pixels (default black). - `intensity` 0-100: 0 = no effect, 100 = full recolor (default 100).

name: list_layer_effects
description: Return the effects currently attached to a layer, with their ids, types, and enabled state. Call this before stacking another effect, before removing one, or whenever you need to know what's already there.

name: remove_layer_effect
description: Remove a specific effect from a layer. Call `list_layer_effects` first to get the `effect_id`. Other effects on the layer are left intact.

name: update_layer_effect
description: Nudge one slot on an existing effect without removing and re-adding it. Use this when the user asks to refine an effect ('a bit more blur', 'darken the shadow', 'rotate the shadow direction') — much cheaper than `remove_layer_effect` + `add_*` and preserves the slot order. **Slot indices** (match the parser order — see add_* tool docs): - Drop shadow: 0=color, 1=opacity (0-255), 2=angle (degrees), 3=distance (px), 4=blur (px) - Gaussian blur: 0=sigma, 1=direction (0|1|2), 2=wrap (0|1) - Fill (color overlay): 2=color, 6=opacity (0-1) - Tint: 0=black color, 1=white color, 2=intensity (0-100) - Tritone: 0=highlight, 1=midtone, 2=shadow, 3=intensity (0-100) Pass `value` as a number for scalar/angle slots and as an `{r,g,b}` triplet for color slots. Call `list_layer_effects` first if you don't already have the `effect_id`.

name: list_themes
description: List the themes embedded in this file. Themes group design-token slots (brand colors, named text strings, etc.). The Default theme is always present; users can add named alternates (e.g. 'Dark', 'Holiday'). Returns `{ themes: [{ id, slot_count, is_active }] }`. Call before `list_slots` if the user references a specific theme by name, or to confirm that any tokens exist before suggesting slot-based edits.

name: list_slots
description: List design-token slots defined in the file. Each slot has ONE stable id (e.g. 'brand-red') but can supply different VALUES per theme — Default theme might have brand-red as crimson, a Dark theme might have it as burgundy. The toolkit renders whichever value the currently active theme provides. Use before inventing hardcoded values whenever the user names a brand concept ('brand red', 'primary blue', 'the header color', 'our headline text'). Filter with `type` to narrow (e.g. COLOR for fill/stroke pickers, TEXT for headline strings). Returns `{ slots: [{ id, type, values_by_theme: { themeId: value, ... }, active_theme, active_value }] }`. Without `theme_id`, `active_value` is what the canvas renders right now. With a `theme_id` filter for an inactive theme, `active_value` may be that filtered theme's fallback value for inspection, while `active_theme` still names the canvas-rendered theme. The `values_by_theme` map shows variants if the user wants to recolor a specific theme. Empty `slots` means the file has no tokens of that type — fall back to inline values and say so.

name: list_motion_system_items
description: Read the user's Motion System library — a separate design library from the file's theme slots. Returns colors / gradients / fonts / easings / durations / motion presets that the user has saved (typically synced from Workflow). Use this when the user names a brand value (e.g. 'brand red', 'standard ease-out', 'fast duration') and `list_slots` did NOT find a match — motion system is the fallback library. The values are returned for inline use (set_fill with the rgb you found, apply_keyframes with the control_points you found, etc.) — they are NOT linked tokens. For multi-property motion presets, use `apply_motion_preset` instead of trying to reconstruct the keyframes. **Hierarchy:** theme slots beat motion-system entries. Always `list_slots` first; only fall through to `list_motion_system_items` on a miss. **Colors vs gradients — same UI section, two enum values.** The Motion System UI shows solid colors AND gradients together under one 'Brand Colors' tab, so a name the user thinks is a 'color' may actually be a gradient (e.g. a logo gradient saved as `clogo`). When the user names a color and `type: 'colors'` returns no match, ALWAYS try `type: 'gradients'` before giving up. Only declare 'not found' after BOTH lookups miss. Returns `{ items: [...] }` typed per family (see schemas below). Pass no `type` to get a summary across all families. Order of `animated_properties` on motion-preset items is not guaranteed; treat as a set.

name: link_slot_to_layer
description: Link an existing design-token slot to a layer's property so the property reads from the slot reference instead of a hardcoded value. Future slot updates propagate automatically (this is the whole point of slots). Call `list_slots` first to find the slot id. **The link is to the slot id, NOT to a specific theme's value.** Whichever theme is active at render time supplies the color/text. If the user later switches themes, the linked layer follows the new theme's value automatically. You never pass a theme id here. What each `slot_type → shape_type` does: - `COLOR` + `shape_type: FILL` (default for shape layers): replaces the layer's fill color with the slot reference. - `COLOR` + `shape_type: STROKE`: replaces the layer's stroke color. - `TEXT` on a text layer: replaces the text content with the slot's string. Ignore `shape_type` for text. - `GRADIENT` + `shape_type: GRADIENT_FILL` / `GRADIENT_STROKE`: replaces the gradient. - `POSITION` / `VECTOR`: links the matching transform property; `shape_type` ignored. - `SCALAR`: links rotation / opacity / skew / skew_axis / stroke_width and REQUIRES `property_context`; `shape_type` ignored. Opacity additionally accepts `opacity_source: 'layer' | 'fill'` and defaults to `'layer'`. Returns `{ slot_id, layer_id, slot_type, shape_type }` on success. Errors if the slot or layer is missing, if `property_context` is missing for SCALAR, or if the slot type is incompatible with the layer (e.g. text slot on a shape layer).

name: create_slot
description: Create a new design-token slot (motion token) by capturing the current value of a layer property. The slot's value comes FROM the layer — you cannot create a slot from an arbitrary RGB/text input. The typical agent flow is: (a) `set_fill` (or set rotation/opacity/scale/etc.) on the layer to the target value, then (b) `create_slot` to capture it as a named token. By default the source layer is linked to the new slot so future updates propagate. **SCALAR slots** (rotation / opacity / skew / skew_axis / stroke_width) share one slot type, so they REQUIRE `property_context` to pick the source property — without it the capture is ambiguous and the call fails. Opacity additionally takes `opacity_source: 'layer' | 'fill'` (defaults to `'layer'`). Returns `{ slot_id, type, theme_id, property_context }`. Errors if the slot name is invalid, already exists, or the layer has no property of the requested kind (e.g., COLOR + FILL on a text layer, SCALAR + rotation on a fully-locked transform). **Slot name rules:** lowercase letters / numbers / underscore / dash, 1–64 chars, must be unique across all themes. If the user gives an unsupported name (spaces, punctuation, uppercase), normalize it (e.g., 'Brand Red' → 'brand-red') and tell them in the reply.

name: create_slot_from_value
description: Create a new COLOR design-token slot DIRECTLY from a value — no source layer required, no scratch-shape dance. Use this when the agent has a `{r, g, b}` in hand (e.g. from `list_motion_system_items`) and wants to register it as a token the user can link future layers to. **When to use this vs `create_slot`:** - `create_slot_from_value`: agent has a value, no source layer. Common after a motion-system lookup: 'tokenize the motion-system primary color' → `list_motion_system_items` → `create_slot_from_value`. - `create_slot`: agent wants to capture a layer's existing fill/stroke/etc. value AND optionally link the source. The traditional flow when the user has selected a layer they want to tokenize from. **Linking is separate.** This tool only registers the slot. To link a layer, call `link_slot_to_layer` afterwards. **Current limitation: COLOR only.** Other slot types (TEXT, GRADIENT, POSITION, VECTOR, SCALAR) still require the scratch-shape pattern via `create_slot`. The tool throws a clear error if you pass a non-COLOR type. Returns `{ slot_id, type, theme_id, value }`. Errors on duplicate name or invalid slot id (lowercase / digits / underscore / dash, 1-64 chars).

name: update_slot_value
description: Change the value of an existing design-token slot in one theme. Every layer linked to the slot updates automatically when that theme is the active one — this is the canonical 'recolor everything that uses brand-red' / 'shift all opacity tokens by 20%' operation. **Themes are per-value scopes.** A slot has one id but multiple values, one per theme. By default this writes to the currently active theme (the one the canvas is rendering). Pass `theme_id` to write to a non-active variant — useful for setting 'Dark' theme colors without leaving the active theme. The response's `applied_to_active_theme: false` plus `note` field tells you when the canvas won't visibly redraw (you targeted an inactive theme). **Provide exactly one value param matching the slot's type:** - `color: { r, g, b, a? }` for COLOR slots - `text: string` for TEXT slots - `gradient: { stops: [{ offset, r, g, b, a? }, ...] }` for GRADIENT slots — stops sorted by offset 0..1 - `position: { x, y }` for POSITION slots - `scale: { x, y }` for VECTOR slots (scale; e.g. `{ x: 100, y: 100 }` for 100%) - `scalar: number` for SCALAR slots — interpreted by the underlying property: degrees for rotation/skew, percent 0..100 for opacity, pixels for stroke_width Rejects type mismatches (e.g. `color` on a TEXT slot) and unknown theme ids. Returns `{ slot_id, theme_id, type, value, applied_to_active_theme, note? }`.

name: unlink_slot
description: Disconnect a layer's property from its design-token slot. The property keeps its current value (frozen at the moment of unlink) but stops following the slot — future `update_slot_value` calls on that slot no longer affect this layer. Use when the user says things like 'detach this from the brand color', 'stop using the token here', 'this one should be one-off', 'break the link'. Returns `{ layer_id, slot_type, shape_type, property_context, unlinked }`. **For SCALAR slots, `property_context` is required** — SCALAR is shared by rotation, opacity, skew, skew_axis, and stroke_width, so the gateway needs to know which property to unlink. For OPACITY specifically, optionally pass `opacity_source: 'layer' | 'fill'` to disambiguate between layer transform opacity and a shape's fill opacity (defaults to `'layer'`).

name: add_theme
description: Create a new theme. The new theme starts with copies of the Default theme's slots (so every slot id continues to render with a value when this theme is active). Use this when the user asks for a 'Dark' / 'Holiday' / etc. variant before customizing values. After creating, the agent typically wants to (a) `select_theme` to make it active, and (b) `update_slot_value({ theme_id, color | text })` per slot to give the new theme its own values. **Naming rules:** lowercase / digits / underscore / dash, 1–64 chars. Convert unsupported user-facing names before calling this tool (for example, 'Holiday Theme' → `holiday-theme`). If there's a collision with an existing theme id, theme-manager appends a suffix and the response returns the actual id used. Returns `{ theme_id, was_renamed }`. `was_renamed: true` means theme-manager picked a different id than requested (collision); surface that to the user.

name: select_theme
description: Switch the currently active theme. The canvas immediately re-renders using the new theme's slot values — every layer linked to a token shifts to the new theme's value for that slot. Use when the user says 'switch to Dark', 'preview the Holiday theme', 'show me what this looks like with the alt theme'. Also useful right after `update_slot_value({ theme_id: 'Dark', ... })` if the user wants to see the change live. Returns `{ active_theme }`. Throws if the theme id doesn't exist.

name: remove_theme
description: Delete a theme and all its per-slot value variants. Slot ids stay; only the per-theme values defined in this theme are removed. The Default theme cannot be removed — that always exists. Use when the user asks to drop a variant they no longer want ('get rid of the Holiday theme'). If the deleted theme was active, the active theme falls back to Default. Returns `{ removed: true, theme_id }`. Throws if the theme is 'Default' or doesn't exist.

name: list_segments
description: List the named animation segments (markers) on the active scene. Each segment is a name + a frame range (start_frame, end_frame). Segments are used by Lottie players to loop / play named ranges and by dotLottie state machines as playback targets. Returns `{ segments: [{ id, name, start_frame, end_frame, duration_frames }] }`. Empty array means the scene has no segments yet. Call before `add_segment` if you need to check for duplicate names, before `add_state` on a state machine that targets a segment, or whenever the user asks 'what segments / loops / chapters does this animation have?'.

name: add_segment
description: Add a named segment (marker) to the active scene's timeline. Segments are reusable named frame ranges — players can loop on one, dotLottie state machines can reference one by name. Returns `{ segment_id, name, start_frame, end_frame }`. The `segment_id` is the toolkit node id; subsequent rename / remove / select calls take this id. **Name uniqueness:** segments don't enforce unique names at the toolkit level, but the agent should avoid duplicate names (state machines reference segments by name and a collision is ambiguous). Call `list_segments` first if unsure.

name: rename_segment
description: Rename an existing segment. Other properties (frames) are unchanged. If state machines reference the old name, they will NOT auto-update — the agent or user must fix those references separately. Returns `{ segment_id, name }`.

name: remove_segment
description: Delete a segment from the active scene. Layer timing and keyframes are NOT affected — segments are pure metadata. If state machines reference this segment, they will break at runtime; clean those up separately. Returns `{ removed: true, segment_id }`.

name: select_segment
description: Set the editor's work-area to a segment's frame range so the user can preview / scrub within it. Visible only in the timeline UI; does not change the underlying segment data. Use after `add_segment` if the user wants to immediately preview the new segment, or when they say 'jump to the intro segment'. Returns `{ segment_id, start_frame, end_frame }`.

name: list_state_machines
description: List the interactivity state machines defined in this file. Each one is `{ id, name, state_count, transition_count, is_active }`. Returns the active state machine id separately as `active_state_machine_id`. State machines are runtime configurations — Lottie players use them to switch playback based on events (click, hover, completion). Most files have 0 or 1 machine.

name: add_state_machine
description: Create a new interactivity state machine. The new (or reused) machine becomes the active one. After creating, add states with `add_state` and link them with `add_transition`. Designate one state as the entry point with `set_initial_state`. **Auto-reuse of empty default machines.** Creator files ship with an empty `StateMachine1`. If you call `add_state_machine` and one or more empty machines (zero states, inputs, and interactions) already exist, this tool reuses the first one — renaming it to your requested name — instead of creating a duplicate. The response includes `reused: true` and `previous_name` so you can mention it (e.g. "I renamed the default empty machine to ..."). Returns `{ state_machine_id, name, reused?, previous_name? }`.

name: set_active_state_machine
description: Switch which state machine is active in the editor. Subsequent `add_state` / `add_transition` calls operate on this one. Returns `{ active_state_machine_id }`.

name: remove_state_machine
description: Delete an entire state machine and all its states / transitions / inputs / interactions. Returns `{ removed: true, state_machine_id }`.

name: list_states
description: List the states in the active state machine. Each is `{ id, name, type, segment, autoplay, loop, mode, is_initial, transitions: [{ id, to_state_id, trigger?, type }] }`. Returns `state_machine_id` and `initial_state_id` at the top level for convenience. Empty array means the active machine has no states yet.

name: add_state
description: Add a new playback state to the active state machine. States represent a playback config — what segment plays, whether it loops, autoplay, etc. The state starts with no transitions; add them with `add_transition`. `segment` references a segment NAME from `list_segments` (not id). If the segment doesn't exist, the player will fail at runtime — call `list_segments` first to verify, or accept that the user might add the segment later. State names must be unique within a machine (case-insensitive — 'Idle' and 'IDLE' collide). Returns `{ state_id, name, segment }`.

name: add_global_state
description: Add a GlobalState to the active state machine. Unlike regular states, a GlobalState's transitions are checked FIRST every tick, regardless of which state is currently active — so they fire from ANY state. Use this when the user says 'from any state when X, go to Y' or 'no matter where we are' or 'always allow Z'. Adding identical transitions to every regular state is the wrong shape — use GlobalState instead. **Constraints:** A GlobalState cannot have incoming transitions (the gateway rejects `add_transition` calls targeting one). Each machine can have at most ONE GlobalState — the gateway rejects a second. Convention names it 'GLOBAL STATE' (uppercase, with space). Returns `{ state_id, name, type: 'GlobalState' }`. Errors on missing active machine, duplicate name (case-insensitive), or attempting to add a second GlobalState.

name: remove_state
description: Delete a state from the active state machine. Any transitions pointing TO this state are automatically removed. If the deleted state was the initial state, the machine loses its entry point — set a new initial state with `set_initial_state`. Returns `{ removed: true, state_id }`.

name: update_state
description: Update fields on an existing state. Only the fields you pass are changed; everything else is preserved. Returns `{ state_id, ...updated_fields }`.

name: set_state_actions
description: Set entry and/or exit actions on a state. Entry actions fire when the state machine ENTERS the state; exit actions fire when LEAVING. Common uses: 'on enter set isPlaying = true, on leave set false', or 'on enter increment session counter'. Semantics: passing `entry_actions: [...]` REPLACES the existing entry array. Passing `entry_actions: []` clears it. OMITTING the field leaves the existing actions untouched — pass only the field you want to change. Actions follow the same 13-shape vocabulary as `add_pointer_interaction` (SetNumeric, SetBoolean, Toggle, Fire, SetTheme, etc.).

name: set_initial_state
description: Designate which state the machine enters first at runtime. Every state machine needs exactly one initial state. Returns `{ initial_state_id }`.

name: add_transition
description: Add a transition from one state to another in the active state machine. Transitions can fire immediately when the from-state's segment completes (no trigger), or in response to an event like 'click', 'pointerEnter', 'pointerExit' (pass `trigger_event`). **If you pass `trigger_event`, you MUST also call `add_pointer_interaction` with a matching `fire_event` — or the transition will never fire at runtime.** `trigger_event` is just a NAME the transition listens for; nothing emits that name until a pointer interaction is wired to fire it. A transition with `trigger_event: 'click'` and no matching `add_pointer_interaction({ pointer_event: 'Click', fire_event: 'click', layer_id })` looks correct in the panel but is dead at playback time. This is the #1 way to ship a broken state machine — always add BOTH calls when using `trigger_event`. The only exception: if a previous interaction in this state machine already fires the same event name, you can reuse it. Default `type: 'Transition'` is immediate. Pass `type: 'Tweened'` with `duration_ms` (number) + `easing` (cubic-bezier 4-tuple) for smooth interpolation between states. Tweened cannot target a GlobalState. Returns `{ transition_id, from_state_id, to_state_id, trigger_event, type }`. Errors if either state id is missing.

name: remove_transition
description: Remove a transition from a state. Returns `{ removed: true, transition_id }`.

name: list_interactions
description: List the interactions defined on the active state machine. Interactions BIND runtime pointer / state events to actions — usually a `Fire` action that emits a named event a transition listens for. **Without an interaction, transition `trigger_event` guards never fire.** If you added an `add_transition({ trigger_event: 'click' })`, you must also `add_pointer_interaction({ pointer_event: 'Click', fire_event: 'click' })` for the click to do anything at runtime. Returns `{ interactions: [{ id, type, layer_name, state_name, actions, fires_event }] }`. `type` is the pointer event name (Click / PointerEnter / …) for pointer interactions OR `OnComplete` / `OnLoopComplete` for state-event interactions. `layer_name` is set for pointer interactions; `state_name` is set for state-event interactions. `actions[]` is the full action list in the agent-facing shape (snake_case + natural value types). `fires_event` is a legacy convenience: it's the input_name of the first `Fire` action when present, otherwise `null` — inspect `actions[]` for everything else.

name: add_pointer_interaction
description: Bind a pointer event (Click, PointerEnter, etc.) on a layer to one or more state-machine actions. This is the wiring that makes `trigger_event` and input mutations actually fire at runtime. Two call shapes — pass EITHER `fire_event` (shorthand) OR `actions[]` (full vocabulary), never both: 1. `fire_event: 'click'` — shorthand for a single `Fire` action against the named event input. Pairs with `add_transition({ trigger_event: 'click' })`. Match exactly, case-sensitive. 2. `actions: [...]` — full action vocabulary. Each action targets an input by name or carries its own value. The 13 action types are: `SetNumeric`, `Increment`, `Decrement` (Numeric inputs); `SetString` (String); `SetBoolean`, `Toggle` (Boolean); `Fire`, `Reset` (Event / any input); `SetFrame`, `SetProgress`, `SetTheme`, `FireCustomEvent` (no input ref); `OpenUrl` (carries `url` + optional `target`). Multiple actions in one interaction fire in order. Action type must match input type (Increment requires Numeric, Toggle requires Boolean, etc.) — the gateway validates and errors clearly on mismatch. **Event input auto-create.** A `Fire` action (whether via `fire_event` shorthand or `actions: [{ type: 'Fire', input_name: 'X' }]`) needs an Event input named `X` to receive the fire — otherwise the fire vanishes and transitions listening for `X` never trigger. To keep this one-call, the gateway AUTO-CREATES any missing Event inputs referenced by Fire actions. The response includes an `auto_created_inputs` array when this happens, so you can surface it to the user (e.g. "Created event input `click` and wired the click handler."). Returns `{ interaction_id, pointer_event, fire_event?, actions?, layer_id, layer_name, auto_created_inputs? }`.

name: add_state_interaction
description: Add a state-event interaction that fires actions when a state's playback reaches a milestone. Use `OnComplete` for 'when this state's segment finishes' or `OnLoopComplete` for 'each time this state's segment loops'. Not to be confused with `add_transition`: a transition WITHOUT `trigger_event` also fires on segment completion, but it transitions to ANOTHER state. Use `add_state_interaction` when you want to fire actions (Fire, Increment, SetTheme, OpenUrl, etc.) on completion WITHOUT changing state. The action vocabulary is identical to `add_pointer_interaction.actions[]` — 13 variants covering input mutations (SetNumeric, Increment, Toggle, …), playback (SetFrame, SetProgress), theme (SetTheme), and side effects (OpenUrl, FireCustomEvent). Action type must match input type or the gateway errors clearly. **Event input auto-create.** Like `add_pointer_interaction`, this tool auto-creates any Event input referenced by a `Fire` action that doesn't yet exist on the active machine. The response includes `auto_created_inputs` when this happens. Returns `{ interaction_id, trigger, state_id, state_name, actions, auto_created_inputs? }`.

name: remove_interaction
description: Remove an interaction from the active state machine. Returns `{ removed: true, interaction_id }`.

name: list_inputs
description: List the typed inputs (variables) on the active state machine. Inputs are how state machines store runtime values — booleans for toggle state, numerics for progress / counters, strings for labels, and events for one-shot triggers. Inputs feed guards on transitions and actions in interactions. Returns `{ inputs: [{ id, name, type, value? }] }`. The `value` is the initial value at machine start (events don't have one).

name: add_input
description: Add a typed input variable to the active state machine. Inputs power guard transitions (e.g. transition fires when `isHovered === true`) and action targets (e.g. an action that sets `progress` to 50). Types: - `Boolean` — initial_value must be 'true' or 'false' (string). - `Numeric` — initial_value must be a stringified number. - `String` — initial_value is a plain string. - `Event` — pure one-shot trigger; do not pass initial_value. Returns `{ input_id, name, type }`.

name: update_input
description: Update an existing input's name or value. Renaming an input also updates all references to it across guards and actions automatically (theme-manager handles the cascade). Returns `{ input_id, name, value }`.

name: remove_input
description: Delete an input. All guards / actions that reference it are also cleaned up automatically. Returns `{ removed: true, input_id }`.

name: import_asset
description: **BEFORE CALLING: check the creation order.** Imported assets are inserted at the TOP of the render stack. If this turn creates multiple layers, emit the calls in BOTTOM→TOP order — the backdrop / sky / base image FIRST, foreground layers LAST. (Reorder APIs exist if needed via `reorder_layer`, but planning the order is cheaper.) Import an SVG, Lottie, or image into the active scene as a new layer. This is the preferred tool whenever the user pastes SVG markup, provides a URL for an image/Lottie, or asks to add an existing asset. Returns the new layer's id so you can immediately animate it with `apply_keyframes`. Provide either `content` (for inline SVG markup) or `url` (for Lottie JSON / image URLs). Optional `name`, `position`, and `scale` are applied after import.

name: vectorize_image
description: Convert an existing PNG/JPG image layer into editable vector shape layers using Creator's vectorizer. Use this when the user asks to vectorize, trace, convert an image/logo/photo to vectors, or make an imported raster image editable. Defaults to the selected image layer when `layer_id` is omitted. The generated vector layers are inserted above the source and selected; after at least one vector layer is created, the original raster is preserved but hidden so it does not render or export twice. Restore it with `set_layer_visibility({ layer_id: source_layer_id, visible: true })` when the user wants to compare or revert.

name: remove_keyframes
description: Remove keyframes from a single property on a single layer. Omit `frame_range` to clear all keyframes on that property; pass `frame_range: { from, to }` to remove only keyframes whose frame falls in the inclusive range. Use this before calling `apply_keyframes` with the same property when you want to fully replace an existing animation rather than merge with it — or just pass `clear_first: true` on `apply_keyframes` for the common case.

name: duplicate_layer
description: Duplicate an existing layer N times and return the new layer IDs. Optional `stagger_frames` offsets each duplicate's timelineOffset by that many frames (i × stagger) — use for stagger/wave effects. Optional `offset` shifts each duplicate's position by (i × offset.x, i × offset.y) — use for arrays and rows. Common flows: - 'make a row of 5 dots spaced 40px apart': duplicate_layer with count=4 (+ the source = 5 total) and offset={x:40,y:0}, then a single apply_keyframes call on the source animates the base motion. - 'stagger 5 letters': duplicate_layer with count=4 and stagger_frames=3; each clone gets timelineOffset = source + i*3. - **2-D grid (rows × cols)**: call duplicate_layer once per row — first call with count=cols-1 and offset={x:tile,y:0} (top row), then for each additional row, call with count=cols-1 on ONE of the top-row tiles and offset={x:0,y:tile}. Or simpler: N serialized calls, one per row, each duplicating a source tile with x-offsets. Do NOT attempt a 2-D grid with a single duplicate_layer call — `offset` is 1-D. Returns an array of `{ layer_id, name }` for the new layers, in creation order. Capped at 24 copies per call.

name: tile_layer
description: Fill the active scene with a grid of copies of a layer. This is the tool to reach for whenever the user says 'tile across the scene', 'fill with a grid of', 'cover with', 'scatter N', or 'pattern the background with'. It ALWAYS uses `Math.floor` for auto cols/rows so tiles never spill outside the scene bounds. Behavior: - `tile_width` / `tile_height` default to the source layer's visual bounds (read via getBounds). For a polygon with outerRadius 50, that's ~100×100. - `cols` / `rows` default to `floor((scene_dim − 2*margin + gap) / (tile_dim + gap))` so the grid exactly fits. Pass either explicitly to override. - Grid is centered inside the `margin`-inset scene rect. - Optional `gap` between tiles (default 0). - Optional `margin` (default 0) to inset the grid from scene edges. - Optional `alternate_flip: true` rotates odd rows by 180° — ideal for triangle tessellation. - Reuses the source layer as cell (0,0); only cols×rows−1 new layers are created. - Hard cap of 144 tiles (12×12) to keep Creator responsive. Throws if exceeded. Example: 'tile this triangle to fill the scene' → one call, no params beyond layer_id. For a 512×512 scene with a 100px triangle: fills as 5×5 with the grid centered.

name: reorder_layer
description: Restack a layer relative to another in the active scene's render order. Use when creation order was wrong or the user asks to put one layer above/below/in-front-of/behind another. Z-ORDER (index 0 = front/top, per read_scene `ordering`): - To put the layer ON TOP of the sibling (visible in front — e.g. a label over a button fill, text over a circle): `position: 'in_front_of'`. - To put the layer UNDER the sibling (behind — e.g. a shadow behind a card, a backdrop behind content): `position: 'behind'`. USE `in_front_of` / `behind` — they say exactly what you mean. The legacy `before` / `after` refer to render-ARRAY position and invert intuitively (`before` the sibling = drawn after it = renders ON TOP); only use them if you're certain. "bring to front" = `in_front_of` the current front layer; "send to back" = `behind` the current back layer. Pass `layer_id` (the layer to move), `sibling_layer_id` (stays put), `position`. The canvas re-renders after the move — verify with `inspect_scene` and check the target isn't `occlusion.likely_hidden`.

name: group_layers
description: Group multiple active-scene root layers by converting them into a nestable precomposition layer. Creator's native shape-group command only groups drawable shapes inside a shape layer, so root-level layer grouping is represented as a precomp. Use this when the user asks to group several layers, package a component, or create a reusable/nestable precomp from existing layers. Pass layer IDs from `read_scene` in the intended visual set.

name: create_shape_group
description: Create an empty group inside an existing SHAPE_LAYER or group. Use this to build composed single-layer components like cards, icons, badges, and shadows without creating many top-level layers. **RESPONSE — keep `group_id`, it is the only way to address the group afterwards:** returns `{ group_id, parent_id, name }`. `read_scene` returns LAYERS, not the shape/group tree inside them, so this response is your only source of the id. Feed `group_id` straight into `add_shape_to_layer({ parent_id: group_id })` to fill the group and into `set_group_transform({ group_id })` to move / fade the whole group as one unit.

name: add_shape_to_layer
description: Add a rectangle, ellipse, polygon, star, or path to an existing SHAPE_LAYER or group.
