Use with create_shape_group to build one composed unit with internal groups. **RESPONSE:** returns `{ parent_id, shape_id, shape, fill_id, stroke_id }` (`fill_id` / `stroke_id` only when you passed `fill` / `stroke`). Keep `shape_id` — it is the `target_id` for `animate_property` on shape geometry (`shape_size`, `rectangle_roundness`, `shape_path`, …), and `read_scene` does not list the shapes inside a layer. If the fill or stroke fails to attach, the whole call is rolled back (the shape is removed) and it throws, so a successful response means every requested piece exists.

name: set_group_transform
description: Set or keyframe a shape group transform/opacity property. Use this when a composed unit has internal groups that should move or fade together. Pass EITHER `value` (a static set) OR `keyframes` (an animation) — the call throws if you pass neither. `keyframes` wins when both are given. Returns `{ group_id, property, keyframes_added }`; `keyframes_added` is 0 for a static `value` set.

name: reorder_shape
description: Restack a child shape or group relative to a sibling inside the same shape container — to fix internal card/icon order without rebuilding the layer. Z-order: `position: 'in_front_of'` draws the node ON TOP of the sibling, `'behind'` draws it under. Use `in_front_of`/`behind` (clear); `before`/`after` are legacy aliases that invert intuitively (`before` = on top).

name: set_layer_time
description: Retime an existing layer on the timeline. Any combination of start_frame, end_frame, and timeline_offset can be set — omitted values stay as-is. - `start_frame` / `end_frame`: when the layer is visible in the parent scene. - `timeline_offset`: how far the layer's internal timeline is shifted (negative = play later). This is the stagger primitive — give each sibling a different offset. Prefer this over `apply_keyframes` on opacity when the user asks to 'delay' or 'stagger' layers — this is cheaper, correct, and doesn't collide with existing opacity animations.

name: retime_keyframes
description: Shift, scale, reverse, evenly distribute, or RE-EASE keyframes on one layer property WITHOUT rebuilding values. Use for timing/feel polish like "shift this 10 frames later", "make the bounce twice as fast", or "make it springier". **To change the EASING / feel (springy, snappy, smoother, bouncy, more/less overshoot) use `operation: 'set_easing'` with `easing` — NOT apply_keyframes.** set_easing swaps only the easing curve and preserves every frame and value. Rewriting the animation via apply_keyframes forces you to restate all values and risks corrupting positions (e.g. collapsing a staggered word onto itself). For a multi-layer cascade (split-text letters, card grid), call set_easing once PER layer — each call is value-safe, so the layout cannot drift. **Every operation reads the property's CURRENT keyframes, rewrites their frames, and puts the same values back — values are never touched by any operation.** The tool throws if the property has no keyframes yet (use `apply_keyframes` to create them first). `operation`, and the parameters each one reads (all others are ignored): - **`shift_frames`** — moves every keyframe by `offset` frames. Positive = LATER, negative = EARLIER. "shift this 10 frames later" = `{ operation: 'shift_frames', offset: 10 }`. **`offset` defaults to 0, so `{ operation: 'shift_frames' }` with no `offset` is schema-valid and does nothing** — always pass it. Frames are clamped at 0, so shifting earlier past the start piles those keyframes onto frame 0 and flattens that part of the motion; check the returned `frames`. - **`scale_time`** — multiplies each keyframe's DISTANCE FROM THE ORIGIN by `scale`: `new = origin + (old - origin) * scale`. The origin is `start_frame` if given, otherwise the property's FIRST keyframe. `scale` must be greater than 0; zero and negative values are rejected before any keyframes change. `scale < 1` = faster/shorter, `scale > 1` = slower/longer. "make the bounce twice as fast" = `{ operation: 'scale_time', scale: 0.5 }`; "twice as slow" = `scale: 2`. `scale` defaults to 1 (no-op) — always pass it. The result is NOT rounded, so a scale that does not divide the spans evenly leaves keyframes on fractional frames (frame 7 × 0.5 = 3.5); prefer factors that land on whole frames. - **`reverse`** — mirrors the frames inside a window: `new = start + end - old`, so the motion plays backwards while keeping the same span. The window defaults to the property's first→last keyframe; pass `start_frame`/`end_frame` to mirror inside a different window. - **`distribute_evenly`** — respaces the EXISTING keyframes at equal intervals between `start_frame` and `end_frame` (defaults: first→last keyframe), keeping their order and values. Use it to kill uneven timing ("even out the spacing", "make the steps regular"). It does not add or remove keyframes. - **`set_easing`** — replaces the easing curve on every keyframe of the property; frames and values are untouched. Requires `easing` (the call throws without it). **RESPONSE:** returns `{ layer_id, property, operation, retimed, frames }`. `retimed` is how many keyframes were rewritten (unchanged from before — this operation never adds or drops keyframes) and `frames` is the full new frame list, sorted. **Check `frames` before saying done:** repeated values mean keyframes collided (clamping at 0, or a `scale` small enough to merge them) and that stretch of the animation is now flat.

name: delete_layer
description: Remove ONE layer from the scene by id. If the scene digest selection is non-empty and the user says 'delete this', 'remove it', 'delete selected', etc., use the selected layer id(s) with this tool. For multiple selected layers, call this tool once per selected id. Returns `{ layer_id, removed: true }`.

name: create_mask
description: Add a mask to a layer. Masks clip the layer's visible content to an arbitrary shape — use for reveal wipes ('reveal from left'), clipping images/Lotties to a shape ('mask this image to a circle'), and any 'show only the part inside' request. For the common shapes, pass one of the shorthands: - `shape: "rectangle"` + `rect: { x, y, width, height }` — axis-aligned rectangle in LAYER-local coordinates. - `shape: "ellipse"` + `ellipse: { cx, cy, width, height }` — center-defined ellipse, width/height being the bounding box. Plugin synthesizes a 4-point cubic bezier approximation (standard kappa constant). - `shape: "path"` + `path: { points: [{vertex:{x,y}, inTan:{x,y}, outTan:{x,y}}...], closed: boolean }` — raw PathData for complex shapes. Coords are LAYER-LOCAL — a rect at (0, 0, 100, 100) covers the top-left 100×100 of the layer's content, regardless of where the layer sits in the scene. Optional `mode` defaults to 'add' (show only inside the mask). Pass 'subtract' to cut a hole. Optional `opacity` (0–100) controls mask opacity; it is not an enable/disable strength. For an ADD mask, opacity 0 makes the masked layer fully transparent and 100 shows the content inside the outline. For a SUBTRACT mask, opacity 0 cuts nothing and 100 fully cuts inside the outline. Use `remove_mask` to restore unmasked rendering. **RESPONSE — this is the ONLY source of a mask id:** returns `{ layer_id, mask_id, shape, mode, opacity }`. `read_scene` does NOT list masks or mask ids, so if you need to address a specific mask later, keep `mask_id` from this response. Everything that takes a mask id also has a first-mask fallback, so a lost id is recoverable on single-mask layers: `update_mask` / `remove_mask` act on the FIRST mask when `mask_id` is omitted, and `animate_property` targets the first mask when both `target_id` and `target_index` are omitted. Animate mask opacity/path with `animate_property({ layer_id, property: 'mask_opacity' | 'mask_path', ... })` — pass `target_id: mask_id` (or `target_index`) only when the layer has MORE THAN ONE mask; otherwise omit both and it uses the first one. `apply_keyframes` targets layer properties only and cannot reach masks. Note `mask_path` keyframe values are whole PathData objects (`{ points: [...], closed }`), not a width — build the full path for each keyframe. Common recipes: - 'reveal from left': rectangle mask at (0, 0, 0, layerH), then animate `mask_path` from a zero-width rect to a full-width one with `animate_property`. - 'circle clip': ellipse mask, cx/cy = layer center, width/height = desired diameter. - 'oval-vignette': ellipse mask slightly inset from layer bounds, opacity 0 → 100 animated with `animate_property` on `mask_opacity`.

name: update_mask
description: Update an existing mask path, opacity, or mode. Use after create_mask when the reveal shape needs tuning without recreating the mask. Only the fields you pass change; omitted fields are left alone. Returns `{ layer_id, mask_id, updated: { path, opacity, mode } }` — each `updated` flag reports whether that field was part of this call.

name: remove_mask
description: Remove one mask from a layer. Pass mask_id when known; otherwise removes the first mask only. Returns `{ layer_id, mask_id, removed: true }`.

name: set_matte
description: Apply a track/alpha matte: use another layer's alpha/shape as the visibility matte for this layer. This is THE premium-reveal primitive — what AE calls 'Alpha Matte'. Typical flow: 1. User has (or you create) the layer to be revealed (the logo, image, text). 2. User has (or you create) a second layer whose shape defines the reveal region (a growing circle, a wipe rectangle, a word-shaped text layer). 3. Call `set_matte({ layer_id: target, matte_layer_id: matteSource })`. The native tool sets `matteSource.isMatte = true` so the matte layer itself becomes invisible in the render while still defining the reveal region. Animate the matte source (position, scale, trim path, etc.) and the target layer is revealed accordingly. Pass `inverted: true` to show the target OUTSIDE the matte shape instead of inside (inverted alpha matte). Common recipes: - 'reveal logo through a growing circle': create ellipse shape → set_matte with matte_layer_id = circle → apply_keyframes on circle.scale 0 → 100. - 'text appears through a gradient sweep': create rectangle → set_matte → animate rectangle x across the text width. - 'punch a hole': set_matte with inverted: true.

name: remove_matte
description: Clear the track matte from a layer.

name: rename_node
description: Rename a layer, shape, group, mask, or scene node by id. Use for cleanup and making generated structures understandable.

name: set_layer_visibility
description: Show or hide one active-scene layer.

name: set_layer_lock
description: Lock or unlock one active-scene layer.

name: flip_layer
description: Mirror a layer horizontally or vertically. Wraps `layer.flip(direction)`. Use for 'mirror this', 'flip horizontally', 'face the other way'. Works on any layer type.

name: align_layer
description: **Use this as your first choice for centering or aligning layers to the scene.** Wraps Creator's own alignment math — the exact same path the property-panel 'align center' / 'align left' / 'align top' buttons run. Works reliably across text, shape, and image layers. `horizontal-center` aligns the layer's visual bounds to the scene's horizontal midpoint; `vertical-center` to the vertical midpoint. For a fully-centered layer, emit BOTH in order: one tool call with `direction: 'horizontal-center'` and then one with `direction: 'vertical-center'`. Same for 'top-left' → `top` + `left`, and so on. **Prefer this over `center_layer({ target })` unless you need to land on a NON-scene-center point** (e.g. a callout at (180, 380)). For brand-new centered text, prefer `create_text({ center_in_scene: true })` — that's even fewer calls. **RESPONSE:** returns `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`, and `scene_fit`. For text layers, `position` is intentionally omitted — `visual_center` is the only placement coordinate that matters.

name: align_layers
description: Align a SET of existing layers to a shared edge derived from the set itself — the multi-layer counterpart of `align_layer` (which only aligns ONE layer to a SCENE edge). Use this to FIX a row/column you (or the user) hand-placed that came out ragged or misaligned: e.g. make a column of labels share a LEFT edge, or a row of icons share a TOP edge. `edge`: which edge to make flush — `left`/`right`/`horizontal-center` (x-axis) or `top`/`bottom`/`vertical-center` (y-axis). Edge-anchored by each layer's RENDERED visual bounds (so text aligns by its real left/right edge, not its baseline anchor). `to` (optional): the coordinate to align to — `min` (leftmost/topmost; default for left/top), `max` (default for right/bottom), `mean` (default for centers), `first` (the first layer's edge), or an explicit number. Guards: refuses layers with ANIMATED position (all-or-nothing) — align BEFORE animating, then `stagger_layers`. Returns `{ aligned, edge, axis, value, layer_ids }`.

name: layout
description: Lay out multiple items in a ROW or COLUMN with EVEN spacing and shared-edge alignment — in ONE call. **Use this instead of hand-placing positions** for any multi-item arrangement: nav menus, button rows, lists, label stacks, feature rows, and especially LEGENDS / swatch grids / spec-sheet rows / icon lists (a swatch legend = a column of `{swatch, label}` row-blocks — hand-placing those overlaps the label onto the swatch). It creates the items (or arranges existing layers), measures each rendered size, and computes even gaps + alignment so the result is correct by construction — no pixel math, no uneven gaps, no ragged edges. `type`: `row` (horizontal) or `column` (vertical). Provide EITHER `items` (to create text/shapes) OR `layer_ids` (to arrange existing layers) — not both. `gap` (default 24): the SINGLE even gap between items. `align` (cross-axis, default `center`): `start` = shared leading edge (left for a column, top for a row — this is how you get a left-aligned list), `center`, `end`. `origin` (default `scene-center`): where the whole block centers — `scene-center` / `top-center` / `bottom-center` / `{x,y}`. Item kinds: `{ kind: 'text', text, font_size?, fill_color?, font_variant? }`, `{ kind: 'shape', shape, size, fill_color?, roundness?, points?, outer_radius?, inner_radius?, stroke? }`, `{ kind: 'layer', layer_id }`, or a NESTED `{ kind: 'block', type:'row'|'column', items:[…], gap?, align?, group? }` — a sub-layout the parent treats as one unit. Use a block to compose multi-row/column layouts in ONE call: e.g. a vertical list of icon+label rows where the icons all share a left edge and the labels all share another → `layout({ type:'column', align:'start', gap:24, items:[ { kind:'block', type:'row', align:'center', gap:16, items:[{kind:'shape',shape:'ellipse',size:{width:32,height:32}},{kind:'text',text:'Create account'}] }, { kind:'block', type:'row', align:'center', gap:16, items:[…'Verify email'] }, { kind:'block', type:'row', align:'center', gap:16, items:[…'Invite your team'] } ]})`. The outer `column align:'start'` flushes each row-block's left edge, so all circles land on one x and all labels on another — no follow-up `align_layers`. A nested block takes `items` only (no `origin`/`layer_ids`); `group:true` on a block makes it one animatable precomp. Max nesting depth 3. **Cards:** add `background:{ fill, roundness?, padding?, stroke?, shadow? }` to a block to drop a rounded panel sized to its content + padding BEHIND it — so a card = panel + content builds in ONE call (never create the content then bolt a panel on top). **`background` works on a block that CREATES its `items`, OR on the top-level `layout` call itself (it wraps the whole layout in one card panel)** — so build the card's content INSIDE the block (`items:[…]`), do NOT pre-create the text/shapes and then arrange them by `layer_ids` and try to wrap them. If you catch yourself doing `create_shape` (panel) + `reorder_layer` (behind) + `add_drop_shadow` around already-made content, STOP — that's the legacy bolt-on this `background` replaces; rebuild the content as `items` inside the block instead. With `group:true` the whole card becomes one animatable precomp you can slide/scale/fade as a unit. `fill` is required (use `fill:'none'` with a `stroke` for an outlined card); `padding` defaults to 24. E.g. a feature card: `{ kind:'block', type:'column', align:'center', gap:12, group:true, background:{ fill:{r:248,g:250,b:252}, roundness:16, padding:24, shadow:{} }, items:[ {kind:'shape',shape:'ellipse',size:{width:48,height:48}}, {kind:'text',text:'Fast'} ] }`. Returns `items` (each with `layer_id`, `visual_center`, `visual_bounds`; a block item also has `kind:'block'` + `child_layer_ids`), `cascade_order` (flattened reading order of staggerable root layers — pass straight to `stagger_layers`), `evenness` (`main_gaps`, `uniform`), and `content_bounds`. Examples: a left-aligned nav = `layout({ type:'column', align:'start', items:[{kind:'text',text:'Home'},…] })`; a feature row = `layout({ type:'row', align:'center', items:[{kind:'shape',shape:'ellipse',size:{width:40,height:40}},{kind:'text',text:'Fast'}] })`.

name: read_keyframes
description: Read the current keyframes on a layer's keyframe-tool properties. Use this whenever the user asks to TUNE, POLISH, or MODIFY an existing animation ('make the bounce snappier', 'slow down the fade', 'shift this 10 frames later', 'make the rotation smoother') — so you can see what's actually there before changing it, instead of rebuilding from scratch. Without `property`, returns a map of the core properties handled by `apply_keyframes` (`position`, `scale`, `rotation`, `opacity`, `fill_color`, trim path fields, and `stroke_width`). With `property`, returns just that explicit core or extended property. Extended properties such as masks, shape paths, gradients, text animator fields, and time mapping must be named explicitly; they are not included in the bulk read. For static (non-animated) properties, `is_animated` is false and `static_value` is returned instead of keyframes. **For `position` on a TEXT layer, `static_value` is the RAW transform (baseline / box-origin anchor) — NOT the visual center. To animate a text position relative to its rest (the only safe way), keyframe from THIS `static_value`, not from `visual_center`. For a settle-into-place entrance, prefer `animate_entrance`, which reads this for you.** Easing in returned keyframes comes through as the raw stored shape: `{ type: "LINEAR" }` or `{ type: "CUBIC_BEZIER", x1, y1, x2, y2 }`. (Named presets are expanded at write-time, so reads only see the resolved bezier coefficients.)

name: copy_animation
description: Copy keyframes from one layer's core keyframe-tool properties onto another. The classic use: 'match this layer's animation to the others,' 'copy the rotation from the big triangle to the small one,' 'give this the same entrance as that one.' By default, animated core properties from `apply_keyframes` are copied — pass `properties` to restrict. Extended `animate_property` fields such as masks, shape paths, gradients, text animator fields, and time mapping are not copied by this tool. Pass `frame_offset` to shift all copied keyframes by N frames, which stacks with this tool for manual staggers (e.g. call copy_animation for each sibling with a different offset). `clear_first_on_target` (default true) replaces any existing keyframes on the target's matching property; pass false to merge. Properties that don't exist on the target layer type (e.g., `fill_color` on a text layer) are skipped with a note in the response rather than erroring the whole call.

name: list_scenes
description: List every scene in the current project plus which one is active. Cheap read. Use when the user refers to scenes by name ('switch to the outro', 'work on the vertical') so you can find the right `scene_id`, or when deciding whether to create a new scene vs. switch to an existing one. Returns active scene id, and for each scene: id, name, size, framerate, duration, layer_count, and is_nestable (whether the scene can be used as a source for a nested scene layer).

name: create_scene
description: Create a new scene (a.k.a. composition / artboard) in the project. Use for 'make a vertical variant', 'add a second scene for the outro', 'new 1080×1920 version', 'start fresh on a new composition'. All fields optional — omit to inherit defaults. If size is omitted, Creator uses its default (typically 1920×1080). Provide explicit size when the user asks for a specific aspect ratio (9:16 → 1080×1920, 1:1 → 1080×1080, etc.). **IMPORTANT**: `activate` defaults to true, meaning the newly created scene becomes the active scene. Any layer IDs you had from before (in history or from a recent read_scene) are INVALID in the new active scene — they belong to the previous scene. Call `read_scene` immediately after this tool before using any layer-targeting tool. If the user wants a new scene without switching, pass `activate: false` and the current scene stays active.

name: switch_scene
description: Switch Creator's active scene. Provide either `scene_id` (exact) or `name` (exact or case-insensitive substring match across scenes). Use `list_scenes` first if you're not sure what's available. **IMPORTANT**: After this tool runs, any layer_id from prior turns is INVALID — those layers live in the scene you just switched away from. Call `read_scene` before using any layer-targeting tool on the new active scene. If you switched temporarily into a selected precomp/source scene, switch back to the original active scene before ending the turn.

name: set_current_frame
description: Move the active scene's playhead to a specific frame. Use this after creating reveal/draw-on/fade-in animations where frame 0 is intentionally invisible (`trim_end: 0`, opacity 0, offscreen position) so the Creator canvas is left on a representative visible frame. This changes the editor preview frame only; it does not add animation keyframes or alter layer timing.

name: set_scene_background
description: Set the PREVIEW background color of the active scene. **This is preview-only — the color is NOT exported with the final animation; exports always have a transparent background.** Use this whenever you want to see how the design reads against a specific surface (e.g. dark mode preview, brand tint preview, contrast check for white-on-X) WITHOUT polluting the scene with a background rectangle layer. **Strongly prefer this over creating a background SHAPE LAYER.** Motion-design convention: animations float on transparency so they can be composited anywhere. Adding a background rectangle layer adds noise, exports unwanted color, and forces the user to delete it if they want to use the animation on a different surface. The only reasons to add a real background SHAPE LAYER are: (1) a gradient or multi-stop background that's part of the design, (2) a contrast issue that can't be solved any other way, (3) the user EXPLICITLY says 'add a background layer' or similar. For every other case (the user says 'on a dark background', 'against a navy backdrop', 'preview on cream', etc.) use this tool — it changes the scene's preview color, leaves the final animation transparent. **REQUIRED, not optional:** when the scene has no background AND you place near-white (luminance > 0.5, e.g. #f8fafc / #ffffff) full-bleed text or fills, you MUST call this in the SAME turn with a dark color (Slate-900 {r:15,g:23,b:42}) — the default preview is white and light text would be invisible. Button labels on a dark button fill are self-contained and do NOT trigger this; only full-bleed text on the canvas does.

name: set_scene_settings
description: Update the active scene size, framerate, duration, and/or origin point. Use for prompts like "make this 1080x1920", "make it 60fps", or "extend to 8 seconds".

name: create_scene_layer
description: Place an existing NESTABLE scene/precomp into the active scene as a SceneLayer (nested composition / component / precomp). Use this for professional card, panel, logo, or UI units only when `list_scenes` reports the source scene has `is_nestable: true`. Important: newly created top-level scenes that report `is_nestable: false`; those cannot be used as scene-layer sources. Do not create a fresh scene and immediately try to place it unless `list_scenes` confirms it is nestable. For generated cards/panels, prefer a single grouped ShapeLayer when no nestable source exists. Provide `source_scene_id` from `list_scenes`, or `source_scene_name` if unique. The layer is created in the current active scene. The source scene cannot be the current active scene — switch to the parent scene first. After creation, animate the returned `layer_id` like any other layer, and apply `set_matte` to this one layer for viewport clipping.

name: break_scene_layer
description: Destructively break an active-scene scene/precomp layer into independent editable layers. Use only when the user explicitly asks to break apart, detach, ungroup, or extract a nested scene. Do not use for normal edits to a precomp/scene layer contents; switch to the source scene and edit there instead.

name: export_lottie
description: Export the active scene as Lottie JSON for debugging. Result content is redacted in audit logs but returned to the tool caller.

name: apply_bounce
description: Drop or lift a layer with physics-correct bounce keyframes. **Use this for any prompt mentioning bounce / drop / fall / land / gravity**. Computes a parametric trajectory: each successive bounce decays in BOTH amplitude and duration, which is the part hand-tuned bounces always miss (uniform-timing decay reads as wrong). **Position-only by design.** Squash-and-stretch is a separate concern — call `apply_squash` afterward if the user explicitly asked for a 'playful' / 'cartoon' / 'springy' bounce. A bare 'bounce' should not deform the layer's scale. Defaults pick a 'snappy but natural' bounce. Tune `elasticity` and `gravity` for feel: - elasticity 0.4 (stiff, settles fast) → 0.85 (cartoony, lots of bounces) - gravity 1500 (floaty) → 12000 (heavy) - max_bounces 4 is visible; >6 is sub-pixel Returns the impact frame numbers in the response under `impact_frames`. These frames are non-uniform (each bounce decays in BOTH amplitude and duration). Any follow-up tool that targets impacts — `apply_squash`, `apply_coupled_shadow` — **must consume this exact array from the response**. Do NOT estimate, do NOT recompute from elasticity/gravity, do NOT call those tools in parallel with `apply_bounce` (they need the response in scope). Sequence: `apply_bounce` → read response → `apply_squash` / `apply_coupled_shadow` with `impact_frames` from that response.

name: apply_squash
description: Add squash-and-stretch scale keyframes at specified impact frames. **Only call this when the user explicitly asks for 'playful' / 'cartoon' / 'springy' / 'squashy' / 'with squash and stretch' on top of a bounce.** A bare 'bounce' should NOT include squash — leave the layer's scale untouched. **CRITICAL — `impact_frames` MUST be the literal array returned by `apply_bounce`'s response. NEVER invent them, NEVER estimate them, NEVER guess at multiples of a frame number.** This tool is SEQUENTIALLY DEPENDENT on `apply_bounce`: emit `apply_bounce` first, READ its response's `impact_frames` array, then pass that exact array into this tool's `impact_frames` parameter. Do not emit both calls in parallel — `apply_squash` is meaningless without the bounce response in scope. The failure mode if you invent frames: squash fires AFTER the ball has already come to rest (impact frames must land exactly on the bounce arcs, which are non-uniform because each bounce decays in BOTH amplitude and duration — you cannot derive them from elasticity/gravity by hand). Given the impact frames (always from `apply_bounce`'s response), emits a 5-keyframe envelope per impact: anticipation stretch (taller, narrower) → squash at impact (wider, shorter) → rebound stretch → settle. Decays the squash strength on successive impacts so the squash fades out as the bounce dies. The scale.x/scale.y inversion is built in (squash widens X, narrows Y). Don't try to add this manually with apply_keyframes — the timing windows have to align with the bounce arcs or the squash flickers between bounces.

name: apply_coupled_shadow
description: Animate an existing shadow layer to track a bouncing object. **Always use this for shadows under bouncing balls** — it solves all five shadow bugs (A: position pinned at ball center, B: shadow wider than object, C: inverted scale direction, D: copying ball.scale onto shadow, E: redundant static keyframes) by computing every value from the ball's existing position keyframes via the rule: `shadow.position.y = ball.y_at_rest + ball_radius` (CENTER, not top) `shadow.scale.x = widthRatio × ball_diameter` (interpolates between apex and impact ratios; flat `scale.y`) `shadow.opacity = inverse of altitude` (impact = brightest, apex = faintest) **Two-layer stacked-solid fill.** A single solid black ellipse reads as a sticker; a radial-gradient ellipse currently can't export with per-stop alpha. Create TWO shadow ellipses (both circular at natural size, same dark slate solid fill `{r:15, g:23, b:42}`) and call `apply_coupled_shadow` once on each: an Outer 'Shadow Edge' layer (`width_ratio_at_impact: 1.35, width_ratio_at_apex: 0.6, opacity_at_impact: 0.30, opacity_at_apex: 0.10`) and an Inner 'Shadow Core' layer (`width_ratio_at_impact: 0.9, width_ratio_at_apex: 0.4, opacity_at_impact: 0.65, opacity_at_apex: 0.25`). Create the Outer FIRST so the Inner (created LAST) lands on TOP of it (Creator inserts new layers at the top of the stack). **REQUIRED FOLLOW-UPS — do not skip:** 1. Call `add_blur` on EACH shadow layer to soften the edge. Use `sigma ≈ ball_diameter × 0.15` (e.g. 12 for an 80px ball, cap ~30). Without blur the shadow reads as a hard ellipse, not as a penumbra. 2. Call `reorder_layer` on EACH shadow layer with `position: 'behind'` and `sibling_layer_id` = the ball's id, to push each shadow BEHIND the ball. New layers ship at the top of the render stack; the shadow needs to be sent back. Without this the shadow paints over the ball. See `motion-patterns.md` → 'Shadow fill' for the full recipe. Reads the ball's animated position to derive `restY` (max y) and impact frames automatically. The shadow ellipse is auto-resized to `ball_diameter × ball_diameter` natural size so scale percentages render at the right physical width — you don't have to compute scale = target_width / natural_width. Prerequisite: the ball must already have animated position (run `apply_bounce` on it first), and both the ball and the shadow must be ellipse SHAPE_LAYERS. **Create the shadow ellipse with CIRCULAR natural size — `{width: ball_diameter, height: ball_diameter}`. Do NOT pre-flatten the shape (e.g. height=24 for an 80px ball).** The flat-on-the-floor look is produced by this tool keyframing a low `scale.y` constant; if you pre-flatten the shape, the blur falloff zone falls outside the visible ellipse and the user sees a flat dark band. The shadow's fill is preserved through this tool (only size + position + scale + opacity are touched), so apply the fill via `set_fill` BEFORE calling this.

name: ask_user
description: Pause and ask the user a clarifying question. The user's pick is returned to you as the tool result `{ answer: string }`. Use this *instead of* asking the question in your prose so the UI can render an interactive chip. When to call: - The answer materially changes what you'll build (style direction, scope, target layer when ambiguous). - A sensible default would be wrong often enough that asking is cheaper than redoing. When NOT to call: - You can pick a reasonable default and proceed. Most turns should NOT ask. - The user already specified the answer in their message. - You're just confirming you understood the task. Kinds: - `kind: "choice"` — render as a row of buttons. Provide 2–5 short, parallel `choices` (≤40 chars each). Use for 'A or B?' picks where each option produces a meaningfully different output. Set `allow_freetext: true` to also offer an 'Other…' fallback. - `kind: "yes_no"` — render as Yes/No buttons. Use for confirming an assumption. - `kind: "open"` — render as a free-text input. Use only when the answer space is too broad for choices. Rules: - Do NOT also restate the question in your text — the chip carries it. - Keep `question` to one short sentence. - For `choice`, choices should be substantively different (not 'fast' vs 'quickly'). - Maximum one ask_user per turn — chains of questions feel like an interrogation.

name: inspect_scene
description: Render PNG snapshots of the active Creator scene at one or more frames so you can SEE what's on the canvas — composition, colors, layout, animation poses. The tool result also includes the current `read_scene` layer state (ids, names, positions, scale, opacity, text metadata, selection, ordering, visual bounds, scene-center deltas, clipping/off-canvas flags, and an `occlusion` block on any layer hidden behind an opaque layer in front of it), so use that state instead of guessing positions or stack order from pixels alone. If a layer you expect to see has `occlusion.likely_hidden`, it is buried (e.g. a label behind a button fill) — do NOT report it as done; reorder it to the front with `reorder_layer`. **The result is structured issues-first:** (1) a VISIBILITY REPORT listing any occluded / off-canvas / empty / hidden layers (or a clean ✓), (2) a readable LAYER MAP in render order (#0 = front), (3) the rendered FRAMES, (4) the full raw layer data last. READ the visibility report first, then VERIFY against the frames — the images are the ground truth. A layer present in the data can still be invisible (occluded, off-canvas, transparent, same-color-on-same-color); never report a layer as done unless you can SEE it in a frame. **ALWAYS pass `frames` explicitly when the scene has motion — never rely on the default single-playhead snapshot.** Frame 0 alone catches almost nothing: most animations start with opacity:0 or off-screen position, so the snapshot looks empty. Use: - **One-shot reveal / pulse / state change**: `frames: [start, peak, resolve]` where `start` is just before the first beat fires, `peak` is the strongest mid-point of the hero motion (usually the end frame of the hero entrance), `resolve` is a few frames after the last beat ends. For a 0 → 22f card entrance with content cascading to f40, use `[0, 22, 45]`. - **Looping animation** (spinner / ambient pulse / rotation / breath): `frames: [0, end*0.25, end*0.5, end*0.75, end]` — five evenly-spaced frames across the loop. A single snapshot can never verify a seamless loop. When to call (REQUIRED): - **After any `apply_keyframes` call that produces motion** — additive or modifying. Use the 3-frame `[start, peak, resolve]` pattern. Yes, even for a 'subtle pulse on one layer' — a new pulse on a layer that's ALREADY animated can collide with the existing entrance motion, and you only catch that by looking. Skipping this is the #1 source of 'I declared done, user opens it and it's broken' failures. - **After any structural change** (new layer, deletion, fill swap, reorder). - The user describes a visual problem ('it looks off', 'too dark', 'overlapping') and you can't tell from `read_scene` alone. - The user references something visual ('move the logo to the left') and you need to see the current layout. When NOT to call: - Simple structural questions ("what layers are on the canvas?") — `read_scene` is cheaper. - Pure data ops with no visual change: `set_text` on an existing string, `read_scene` to check layer ids, scene metadata fetches. - Do NOT inspect mid-change between every micro-call. Batch your apply_keyframes / create_shape calls, THEN one 3-frame inspect at the end. Defaults: - `frames` omitted → snapshots the current playhead (RARELY what you want — see above). - `scale` omitted → 1× native scene size. - `background_color` omitted → transparent (the scene's own background renders if it has one). Limits: at most 6 frames per call, scale clamped to [0.25, 2].
